title: Budapest in 3 days: a relaxed first-time itinerary
description: A practical three-day Budapest itinerary covering Castle Hill, Parliament, the Danube and a thermal-bath afternoon, with room to explore.

heroImage.alt: Panorama from the Buda hills across the Danube to the Chain Bridge, Parliament and the Pest skyline

intro: Three days give you room for Budapest’s big sights and some unplanned discoveries. This suggested route groups nearby places, keeps the Buda and Pest sides together where practical and leaves one afternoon for slowing down. Treat the order as a starting point, then move any timed visits around the tickets you actually secure.
highlights: Day 1: Castle Hill and the Buda riverbank
Day 3: City Park and a thermal-bath visit

children.text: Choose one or two visits that matter most to you and arrange those first. Parliament’s official visitor service directs online ticket buyers to Jegymester; use that official route rather than choosing a reseller by its name alone. If the available tour falls on a different day, swap the days of this itinerary.

Keep arrival day light if you land late. A riverside walk and dinner can be a better first evening than trying to fit a major interior visit between the airport journey and hotel check-in. The timings here are our planning suggestions, not tour departure times.
Save the official venue pages for your travel dates.
Keep a weather-flexible indoor option in reserve.
Browse our attraction pages for details on places that interest you.

sections.title: Day 1 — Castle Hill and a Buda panorama

children.text: Begin around Trinity Square and Matthias Church, then spend time at Fisherman’s Bastion. The lower level and upper lookout have separate admission arrangements: the district’s visitor guide lists the lower level as free and the upper lookout as paid. You do not have to buy an upper-level ticket simply to enjoy the wider district.

Continue through the Castle District instead of rushing straight back down. We suggest allowing a half-day for sightseeing, pauses and an optional interior visit. Walk a stretch of the Buda riverbank later for a view towards Parliament. If slopes or uneven surfaces are difficult, plan the approach with BKK and check each venue’s access arrangements.

Build the morning around Parliament if you have a confirmed visit. Otherwise, admire the exterior around Kossuth Square and continue with a Pest-side walk. Do not turn up assuming an interior ticket will be available on arrival.

Leave the afternoon for downtown streets and a café stop. Keep a meal break in the plan rather than treating food as something to squeeze in between sights. Finish with another riverfront perspective; a cruise is an optional alternative, so compare its departure point and inclusions before booking.

sections.title: Day 3 — City Park and time to unwind

children.text: Make the third day deliberately slower: a walk in City Park followed by a bath visit if it suits your group. Széchenyi is the natural pairing for this area, but check the current entry conditions before building the day around it.

Gellért Bath is currently closed for renovation, so it is not an alternative stop on this route. If bathing is not right for your group, extend the park visit or revisit your favourite neighbourhood. Leave a buffer before an airport transfer rather than planning a final paid activity against a tight departure.

sections.title: Make the route work for you

children.text: With two days, choose Castle Hill plus downtown Pest and treat the baths as a swap, not an extra obligation. With a fourth day, repeat a neighbourhood at a different pace before adding a distant excursion.
This route is self-guided and does not calculate live travel times. Check the day’s transport service and venue notices, especially if your plans depend on a particular connection or entry slot.

sections.title: The landmarks on this route, at a glance

children.text: A few facts help you pace the three days. The Hungarian Parliament was begun in 1885, inaugurated in 1896 for the millennium celebrations and completed in 1904; you see its interior on a guided visit arranged through the official visitor centre. St. Stephen's Basilica is 96 metres tall, as tall as Parliament, and its dome can be reached by lift or by 304 steps.

Heroes' Square marks the thousandth anniversary of the Magyar settlement: the Millennium Monument was begun in 1896 and inaugurated in 1905. Széchenyi Thermal Bath opened in June 1913 and is fed by two thermal springs, one at 74 °C and one at 77 °C. The Great Market Hall at Fővám tér opened on 15 February 1897.
Parliament: arrange a guided visit through the official visitor centre before you travel.
Basilica: the church and the dome terrace have different visiting hours; check the current ticket options on the official site.
Széchenyi: the nearest Metro line 1 stop is Széchenyi fürdő, beside the entrance.

sections.title: Széchenyi: what to know before you go

children.text: Széchenyi has rules that can change a group's plan, so read the bath's own FAQ before you build Day 3 around it. Children under 14 have not been able to visit since 1 August 2025, and the bath points families towards other Budapest baths. The daily ticket does not include swimwear, towels, bathrobes, slippers or swimming caps. You can buy some items in the shop or bring your own, and rental is not available. Slippers are mandatory, and a cap is required only in the lap pool.

Only swimwear made for swimming is allowed in the pools, and you may not bring in alcohol. For luggage, the bath recommends a private cabin for suitcases and larger bags; the lockers are small and suit a backpack. The building is not fully barrier free, and a guest with a wheelchair is asked to request a private changing room big enough to keep the chair in. The bath posts maintenance notices on its website, so check there on the morning you go.

St. Stephen's Basilica is a working church. Its visitor policy says liturgical functions take precedence over tourist access, so visiting times can change. Cover your shoulders and knees: the policy says inappropriate clothing may lead to refusal of entry. Do not eat, drink alcohol or smoke inside, stay on the designated routes and expect your bag to be checked on entry or exit. The ticket does not cover safekeeping of belongings, so travel light.

The dome terrace is 65 metres up. The basilica's official page says lifts were installed in 2003 and that the stairs have 304 steps, so the climb is optional. For getting around, BKK says that over 90 per cent of its buses are low-floor and that every Metro line 4 station is step-free, while low-floor trams run on only about 30 per cent of tram lines. Its journey planner can show accessible routes. BKK's accessibility page does not cover Metro line 1 or Castle Hill, so contact BKK before you rely on either.

faqs.question: Is three days enough for a first visit?
faqs.answer: It is a useful starting length for this suggested route. Choose fewer interior visits if you prefer a slower pace or have limited mobility.

faqs.question: Does this itinerary include booked tickets?
faqs.answer: No. It is a self-guided planning suggestion. Arrange tickets separately through the venue or a provider you choose.

faqs.question: Can children visit Széchenyi Thermal Bath?
faqs.answer: Not at present for the standard visit: the bath's own FAQ says children under 14 have not been able to visit since 1 August 2025, and it recommends other Budapest baths for families. Check that page before you plan.

faqs.question: Do I have to climb to the top of St. Stephen's Basilica?
faqs.answer: No. The basilica's official page says the 65-metre panorama terrace can be reached by lift, which was installed in 2003, or on foot by 304 steps.

title: Budapest thermal baths: choosing your first visit
description: Plan a Budapest bath visit with practical notes on Széchenyi, Rudas, age restrictions, what to pack and the Gellért closure.

heroImage.alt: Bathers in the turquoise outdoor pool below the yellow facade of the Széchenyi Thermal Bath
heroImage.caption: Budapest city panorama — this is not a photograph of a bath.

intro: Choose a bath around the kind of day you want, where you are staying and who is travelling with you. A well-planned visit needs more than an entrance ticket: check which areas it covers, the admission rules and what you need to bring. Here is a practical starting point for your first Budapest bath visit.
highlights: Pair Széchenyi with a City Park day
Check the exact Rudas session before choosing tickets
Gellért is currently closed for renovation

sections.title: Choose around the rest of your day

children.text: Our suggested approach is to give the bath a dedicated part of the day. Avoid squeezing it between two fixed-time attractions: changing, settling in and travelling to the next stop all take time. Choose somewhere convenient to your sightseeing rather than crossing the city for an activity you feel obliged to do.

Széchenyi is a straightforward candidate for a day centred on City Park. Rudas is worth considering when you are planning time on the Buda side. Those are itinerary pairings, not a ranking or a promise about crowd levels.

sections.title: Széchenyi: check the practical details first

children.text: Széchenyi’s official FAQ says children under 14 have not been able to visit since 1 August 2025, unless a rheumatologist’s or orthopaedic doctor’s certificate has been sent for approval in advance. It also states that the building is not fully barrier-free. Check the current instructions directly if either point affects your party, rather than assuming a standard ticket meets your needs.

Compare the available ticket types on the official bath site. Do not assume that a locker, private changing cabin or optional experience is interchangeable. Read the description of the ticket you are about to buy and keep the confirmation accessible.

sections.title: Rudas: the session and access areas matter

children.text: Rudas publishes different access arrangements across the week, including single-sex sessions for the Turkish bath. Check the date, session and included areas together before choosing a ticket, especially when visiting as a couple or group.

The operator states that children under 14 cannot visit. Its schedule and ticket page list night bathing as a separate session with its own night ticket, so check which evenings it runs. Avoid relying on a general opening-hours snippet when your plan depends on a particular area being accessible.

sections.title: Gellért: remove it from your current bath plan

children.text: The official Gellért website says the bath has been closed since 1 October 2025, with reopening planned for 2028. A planned reopening is not a confirmed date for a future booking.

Older destination articles and photographs may still suggest visiting. If this bath is the reason for a future trip, wait for an operator announcement before making non-refundable plans around its return.

As a practical packing list, take swimwear, a towel, suitable poolside footwear and a bag for wet items. Check the venue’s specific rules for any additional equipment or rental options before relying on them. Keep valuables to a minimum and follow changing-room instructions.

Plan a pause afterwards instead of a sprint to the next attraction. If you are travelling with children, choose a venue explicitly suitable for their ages and confirm which facilities they can use. A famous thermal bath is not automatically a family swimming-pool option.
Read the operator’s current admission rules.
Check exactly what the ticket covers.
Match the visit to your group’s ages and access needs.

Budapest's bathing culture is older than any of the buildings you will visit. The Rudas Baths were founded in 1571 or 1572 under Ottoman rule, commissioned by Sokollu Mustafa Pasha, and still keep an Ottoman dome and an octagonal pool. The Lukács Baths say that thermal baths have been used on their site since at least the twelfth century, reportedly by the Knights Hospitallers.

The two best-known buildings are much younger. The Széchenyi Thermal Bath opened in June 1913 in a neo-Baroque palace designed by Győző Czigler and completed after his death by his associates, and the Gellért Thermal Bath was built between 1912 and 1918 in the Secession (Art Nouveau) style, together with its hotel. Gellért has been closed for refurbishment since October 2025, with reopening planned for 2028, so do not plan around it.

Széchenyi’s FAQ is a good guide to the conventions at a large Budapest bath. Only swimwear designed for swimming is allowed in the pools, so jeans, leggings or underwear will not do, and nude bathing is not permitted. Slippers are mandatory. The daily ticket does not include towels, bathrobes, slippers, swimwear or caps, and rental is not available, so bring your own or buy them in the shop.

Swimming caps are required only in pools marked with a pictogram, which the page links to the lap pool; Rudas also says caps are mandatory in its swimming pool. In saunas, sit on a towel and leave phones and smartwatches outside unless staff allow them. Razors are prohibited throughout the bathing area, and alcohol is not allowed. You exchange your QR code for a wristband on arrival and keep it until you leave. Rules differ between baths, so read your own bath’s page first.

sections.title: Beyond the famous baths: Lukács, Palatinus and families

children.text: Lukács is a practical Buda-side alternative. Its history page says Knights of the Order of St. John settled there in the twelfth century and that in 1979 it opened Budapest’s first daytime hospital offering complex thermal treatments. Its website lists pools, a Sauna World and medical treatments, so it feels like a working spa as much as a sightseeing stop. The pages we opened state no age rule, so confirm one before bringing a child.

Families need extra care. Xpat Loop reports that, under Government Decree 510/2023, children under 14 may not bathe in medicinal pools unless a doctor prescribes it, and that Palatinus on Margaret Island stays open to children year-round under parental supervision. Palatinus began in 1919 as a Danube beach, became an open-air bath in 1921, and today describes spa, open-air and wave-bath facilities with 15 pools. Confirm current rules with the operator.

sections.title: What is in the water: temperatures and time

children.text: Széchenyi draws on two springs. According to Wikipedia, the first artesian well, drilled between 1868 and 1878, reached water of about 74.5 degrees Celsius at 970 metres, and a second spring found in 1938 delivers about 77 degrees. Those figures describe the springs, not the pools, which are kept cooler.

Rudas shows what that looks like in practice. Its pools page lists six thermal pools in the Turkish bath at 16, 28, 30, 33, 36 and 42 degrees, with a recommended bathing time of 20 minutes, plus a 36-degree panorama pool with views of the Danube. The swimming pool is kept at 29 degrees. Treat the recommended time as a guide, and leave the hottest pool until you know how you feel.

faqs.question: Is Gellért Bath open?
faqs.answer: The operator says it is closed for renovation, with reopening planned for 2028. Check the official notice before making future plans.

faqs.question: Can children visit Széchenyi or Rudas?
faqs.answer: Rudas states that under-14s cannot visit. Széchenyi publishes an under-14 medical-certificate and approval exception. Always read the operator’s current admission conditions.

faqs.question: Do I need a swimming cap in Budapest baths?
faqs.answer: Only in some pools. Széchenyi requires caps in pools marked with a pictogram, which its FAQ links to the lap pool, and Rudas says caps are mandatory in its swimming pool. Bring one if you plan to swim lengths.

faqs.question: Can I rent towels, swimwear or slippers at Széchenyi?
faqs.answer: Széchenyi says rental is not available. The daily ticket does not include towels, bathrobes, slippers, swimwear or caps, so bring your own or buy them in the bath’s shop.
